strengths: Scale and annotation quality: M4Human provides 999 sequences / ~661K synchronized frames / ~15.3 h over 20 subjects and 50 actions, which is ~9× the prior largest radar HMR dataset (mmBody, ~20 subjects but far fewer frames/actions). Ground truth comes from a 37-marker Vicon MoCap system plus human-in-the-loop cleanup and SOMA-based SMPL-X fitting, rather than noisy RGB-derived pseudo-labels used by most prior radar datasets (mRI, mm-Fi, MARS). This directly addresses a recognized bottleneck in RF-based human sensing.

Genuinely new modality support: the dataset releases both raw radar tensors (RT) and processed radar point clouds (RPC) with calibrated extrinsics and time synchronization, enabling research at different levels of RF signal processing. The motivating observation that RPC discards most of the signal (effective RPC ratio 87.0% for M4Human vs 6.2% for mmBody) is a concrete, quantified justification for the RT modality and for the dataset's human-centric radar configuration (20 Tx/Rx, 7 GHz, 62–69 GHz).

Action and motion diversity beyond prior work: the 50 classes span in-place daily activities, clinically motivated rehabilitation exercises, and non-in-place sports (basketball, badminton, boxing). This is a meaningful step past the sit/walk-only scope of mRI, mm-Fi, mmBody, etc., and enables the harder P3 (non-in-place) protocol.

A reasonable, efficient RT-based baseline: RT-Mesh (2D BEV localization → 3D RoI-selected transformer → SMPL-X head) is the first HMR method operating directly on raw radar tensors, and its reported 2.74 ms latency / 2.60 GFLOPs versus 39.58 ms / 50.67 GFLOPs for RT-Pose shows it is practical for edge deployment while matching or exceeding RPC/RT baselines on MVE/MJE.

Benchmark breadth and honest reporting: three protocols (in-place, sit-in-place, non-in-place) and three splits (random, cross-subject, cross-action), plus data-scaling curves (25/50/100%), single- vs multi-modal comparisons (RGB, depth, RPC, RT and fusion), and a downstream skeleton-based HAR study. The paper does not hide that radar-only MVE (~70–90 mm) and cross-subject/cross-action performance are still far from camera-based HMR, and it reports TE advantages of radar over RGB, which is a non-trivial and plausible finding given radar's sensitivity to moving foreground.

The capture pipeline is described with enough specificity to be credible: PnP-based extrinsic calibration with non-coplanar MoCap markers and radar corner reflectors, trigger-gesture-based temporal alignment between the 12 Hz sensor stream and 100 Hz Vicon stream, and per-frame overlay verification of RGB-D/RPC against the reconstructed mesh.
weaknesses: The central motivation—robustness to occlusion and adverse illumination, and privacy preservation—is never experimentally validated. There is no experiment in which the RGB/depth camera fails (subject occluded by furniture/clothing, low light) while radar still succeeds, even though this is the primary argument for radar-based HMR. Conversely, the dataset includes RGB and depth, and all subjects are recorded in a single controlled room, so the privacy claim is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Annotation quality is claimed ('high-quality', 'high-precision') but never quantified. No calibration residual, marker-tracking error, SOMA fitting error, or comparison against an independent reference (e.g., markerless multi-view) is reported, and there is no analysis of how MoCap noise propagates into the mesh GT used to supervise all benchmarks. For a dataset paper this is the most important missing evidence.

Environment and subject diversity are limited: all data come from one ~6 × 5.5 m² room with a fixed sensor tripod and a single radar placement; 20 subjects within 1.5–1.8 m and 45–90 kg, all wearing caps/masks. Since mmWave returns are strongly environment-dependent (multipath, background clutter), generalization to new rooms/sensor placements is untested, which limits the practical value of the 'benchmark' framing.

Dataset statistics that matter for usability are absent: total storage size (particularly for the 4D RT tensors, T=4 × 121 × 111 × 31 per sample), per-modality file formats, and download/processing instructions are not given in the main text. Given that RT is the paper's headline modality, its practical cost is under-specified.

Baseline comparison breadth is thin. Only one RGB method (TokenHMR) and one depth method (P4Transformer) are used as camera-based references, and only two RPC methods (mmMesh, P4Transformer) plus two RT-adapted HPE methods (MMVR, RT-Pose, RETR). No radar-domain HMR method beyond the authors' own baseline is trained, so the claim that M4Human 'establishes benchmarks' is only partially supported; results are also single-run with no variance or significance reporting.

Architectural and training details are deferred to the supplementary (losses, 2D-to-BEV reshaping of the 4D temporal tensor, RoI cropping, hyperparameters, training schedule), making the RT-Mesh baseline hard to assess from the main paper. In particular, it is unclear how the T=4 temporal context is preserved when the 4D RT tensor is collapsed into a 2D BEV map, which could be a source of the residual error on fast, non-in-place motions.

The multimodal fusion study is superficial: 'intermediate feature concatenation before the HMR head' is a single simple scheme, and the paper draws conclusions about complementary modality value from it without exploring alternatives (e.g., cross-attention, per-modality distillation). The claim that 'learning jointly from two radar representations is mutually reinforcing' rests on a narrow experiment.

Table 1 has apparent inconsistencies in the modality/annotation check marks (e.g., entries under 'RGB'/'Depth'/'mmWave' for datasets that do not obviously provide them, and annotation columns marked '3D*' without explanation of the asterisk beyond a footnote). The comparison table is the paper's core positioning evidence, so these ambiguities weaken the 'largest/first' claims that should be precisely verifiable.

Downstream HAR results (RT-estimated skeletons: 64.82% Top-1 vs 75.67% GT) show a substantial gap and are reported without any follow-up analysis of which actions fail or why, limiting the practical takeaway for the community the benchmark targets.

strengths: The paper introduces M4Human, a large-scale multimodal mmWave radar dataset for human mesh reconstruction with 999 sequences, ~661K synchronized frames, 20 subjects, and 50 action classes, making it ~9x larger than prior largest radar HMR dataset. This is a substantial and timely contribution to privacy-preserving RF-based human sensing.

The dataset provides four synchronized modalities—RGB, depth, raw radar tensors (RT), and radar point clouds (RPC)—enabling research across different RF signal granularities. This is valuable because prior radar datasets typically provide only sparse RPC or limited RT.

High-quality MoCap-based annotations are a core strength: marker-based Vicon capture with 37 markers, human-in-the-loop cleanup, SOMa mesh reconstruction, and manual verification yield dense SMPL-X mesh, pose, and global trajectory labels, which are much richer than noisy RGB-derived pseudo-labels used in prior RF datasets.

The benchmark is comprehensive, covering multiple protocols (in-place, sit-in-place, non-in-place), three split settings (random, cross-subject, cross-action), four metrics (MVE, MJE, MRE, TE), and comparisons across RPC, RT, RGB, depth, and fusion methods.

The proposed RT-Mesh baseline is simple but effective for RT-based HMR, achieving strong accuracy and high efficiency (2.74 ms latency, 2.6 GFLOPs), and the scaling analysis demonstrates that larger training data consistently improves cross-subject and cross-action generalization.

The paper convincingly shows that radar-only HMR can approach RGB-D performance in some settings, especially for translation error, and that fusing radar with RGB or depth yields consistent gains. This supports the practical value of mmWave radar as a complementary modality.

The manuscript is generally well organized, with a clear system overview, calibration/synchronization description, dataset comparison table, and downstream HAR evaluation that further demonstrates utility.
weaknesses: Annotation quality is not quantitatively evaluated. The paper relies on Vicon markers plus SOMa for mesh reconstruction but does not report marker residual errors, mesh fitting errors, or a quantitative validation of the final SMPL-X annotations, which are critical for a benchmark dataset.

The RT-Mesh baseline has limited methodological novelty: it combines a 2D BEV transformer for localization with a 3D RoI-selected transformer for mesh regression, which is a reasonable but incremental adaptation of existing HPE/HMR designs rather than a fundamentally new approach.

Table 2 contains apparent citation inconsistencies: mmMesh is listed as [44] although the text identifies mmMesh as [43], and P4Trans is cited as [7] while the text describes P4Trans as [14] applied to mmBody [7]. These should be corrected.

Experimental results lack statistical significance analysis or variance estimates. Most tables report single numbers without error bars or repeated runs, making it difficult to judge whether small differences between methods are meaningful.

Multimodal fusion is limited to intermediate feature concatenation. More advanced cross-modal fusion strategies are not explored, so the paper's conclusions about fusion benefits are suggestive but not exhaustive.

The dataset includes RGB and depth data, which may still raise privacy concerns despite de-identification efforts such as caps and masks. The paper should clarify data access restrictions and consent procedures for the RGB-D portion.

Main-paper details for RT-Mesh architecture and training losses are deferred to the supplementary material. Reproducibility depends heavily on the promised code/data release and supplementary details, which are not fully assessable from the manuscript alone.
The dataset contains 20 subjects, which is reasonable for a radar dataset but still limits diversity; cross-subject performance drops notably in S2, showing that generalization remains challenging.

strengths: M4Human is a genuinely large-scale multimodal dataset: 999 sequences, ~661K synchronized frames (~15.3h), 20 subjects, and 50 actions, roughly 9x larger than the prior largest RF-based HMR dataset (mmBody). It uniquely releases both raw radar tensors (RT) and radar point clouds (RPC) alongside synchronized RGB and depth, filling a real gap for privacy-preserving RF-based human sensing.

The capture and annotation pipeline is carefully engineered: 37-marker Vicon MoCap, cross-modal calibration via PnP with checkerboard/corner reflectors, trigger-gesture-based time synchronization, and human-in-the-loop cleanup of marker trajectories. This is a solid infrastructure contribution.

Action diversity extends beyond the simple in-place motions of prior radar datasets to include rehabilitation exercises and non-in-place sports (e.g., basketball, badminton), enabling more challenging dynamic motions and broader downstream tasks.

The benchmark is broad: RPC vs. RT comparison, three protocols (in-place/sit-in-place/non-in-place), three splits (random/cross-subject/cross-action), comparison against RGB-D methods, multimodal fusion, a dataset-scale study, and a downstream HAR benchmark.
The RT-Mesh baseline is the first HMR method to operate directly on raw RTs and is very efficient (2.74ms, 2.6 GFLOPs), making it practical for edge deployment.
The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with informative figures and tables.
weaknesses: The central 'high-fidelity'/'high-quality' GT claim is not quantitatively validated. The mesh GT is produced by SOMA, a learned marker-to-body reconstructor, and is only checked visually (spatial-temporal alignment). For a benchmark whose value depends on GT fidelity, SOMA's error on this data should be quantified (e.g., held-out markers or multi-view consistency); otherwise the reported absolute MVE values conflate model error with GT error.

Several claims are overstated. 'RT-Mesh ... exceeds reported results on prior radar-based HMR/HPE datasets' (Sec. 5.1) is a cross-dataset comparison that is not meaningful given different GT, sensors, and protocols. Likewise, the claim that radar-only models are 'comparable' to RGB-D rests on single-run numbers without variance.

Baseline fairness is unclear: mmMesh and P4Transformer were designed for mmBody, and it is not stated clearly whether they were retrained on M4Human, while RT-Pose and RETR are HPE methods retrofitted with HMR heads. The comparison may not reflect each method's best performance.

Methodological novelty is limited: RT-Mesh is a standard two-stage pipeline (2D BEV localization + 3D RoI transformer) with architecture and loss details deferred to the supplementary, and its gains over RPC baselines are modest and inconsistent (Table 2).
No variance/error bars or significance tests are reported; all results appear to be single runs, which weakens the comparative conclusions.

The 'unconstrained indoor scenarios' claim is questionable: data were captured in a fixed lab setup with a tripod-mounted sensor and overhead Vicon, with subjects constrained to 0.5-6m and a ~6x5.5m area.
Data and code 'will be released after the paper publication' with no anonymous access, so reproducibility cannot be assessed at review time.
The subject pool (20 subjects, essentially one sequence per subject-action pair) may be limited for the strong cross-subject generalization claims.

strengths: Significant and well-motivated dataset contribution: M4Human provides 661K synchronized frames across 999 sequences and 20 subjects with 50 diverse actions, claimed to be ~9× larger than the prior largest mmBody, and is the first benchmark to support RT-based (raw radar tensor) HMR in addition to RPC.

High-fidelity ground truth: annotations are derived from a marker-based Vicon MoCap system with a 37-marker setup and human-in-the-loop cleanup, then reconstructed with SOMA into SMPL-X meshes and global trajectories. This avoids the noisy pseudo-GT from RGB-D that plagues prior RF datasets, as clearly argued in the related work and Table 1.

Genuinely diverse action set spanning 30 in-place daily/rehab, 5 sit-in-place, and 15 non-in-place dynamic sports movements, with subjects allowed substantial free-space translation—this directly addresses the limitation of prior radar datasets that focus on simple in-place actions.

Multi-granularity radar data (both raw RT and processed RPC) is released, enabling research at different levels of RF signal processing and representation learning, and the paper convincingly motivates the complementary value of RT (denser spatial context) versus RPC (salient returns).

Comprehensive benchmarking: three splits (random, cross-subject, cross-action), four protocols, single-modality and fusion comparisons against RGB, depth, RPC and RT baselines, a dataset-scale study demonstrating scaling-law behavior, and downstream HAR/HMP evaluation. This is considerably broader than typical dataset papers.

Practical engineering contributions are documented, e.g., the LMDB-based sparse-compressed data pipeline that reduces storage from ~20 TB to ~150 GB and per-epoch loading from >18 hrs to <1 hr, which materially improves usability of the large-scale data.

The privacy-preserving motivation is well-justified and ethically handled (de-identification with masks, ethics statement), and the paper appropriately positions mmWave as a complement/alternative to LoS vision.

The proposed RT-Mesh baseline is efficient (2.74 ms latency, 2.6 GFLOPs) and demonstrates that RT-based HMR is feasible with a compact two-stage BEV-localization + 3D-RoI architecture, supporting deployment on edge devices.
The manuscript is clearly written and organized, with helpful figures (system setup, calibration, synchronization, qualitative comparisons) and honest acknowledgment of remaining challenges.
weaknesses: Cross-subject generalization is a central claim but the dataset has only 20 subjects, and the scaling study's S2 setting trains on as few as 4 subjects; this limits how strongly subject-generalization conclusions can be drawn, and the reported S2 performance drops substantially.

RT-Mesh has limited methodological novelty—it is essentially a 2D BEV transformer plus a 3D RoI transformer, and the authors themselves frame it as 'a simple but effective baseline.' It is not the best-performing method (e.g., RT-Pose achieves lower MVE on S1 ALL: 87.0 vs 90.9 for RT-Mesh), so the algorithmic contribution is modest.

The body-shape parameter β is reported as inaccurate and temporally inconsistent, which weakens the 'mesh' reconstruction claim; in practice the method largely recovers pose. This limitation is acknowledged but not quantified with shape-specific metrics beyond the aggregate MVE.

Generalization to unseen actions/subjects degrades notably (S2/S3), and while the paper reports this, it offers little analysis of why specific actions (e.g., side lunges, boxing) fail beyond generic statements about needing 'stronger human priors.'

Comparisons to RGB(D) methods depend on fine-tuning decisions (e.g., TokenHMR fine-tuned, P4Transformer for depth) that may not be equally optimized across modalities, and all evaluation is confined to the authors' own dataset, so the relative standing of modalities could be dataset-specific.

Analysis of radar-specific failure modes (multipath, chair-induced noise, self-occlusion, body-part miss-detection) is largely qualitative; a more systematic characterization would strengthen the benchmark's diagnostic value.

The dataset's public availability and the reproducibility of baselines cannot be verified from the manuscript alone, and the RT baseline relies on the supplementary for architecture/loss details, which constrains full assessment of the method.

strengths: Substantial and well-motivated dataset contribution: M4Human is the first benchmark to support RT-based (raw radar tensor) human mesh reconstruction, providing 661K synchronized frames (~9× larger than the prior largest mmBody) across four aligned modalities (RGB, depth, RPC, RT). This directly addresses a genuine gap—prior RF datasets offer only sparse skeleton annotations from coarse HPE, and no prior work supported RT-based HMR.

High-quality, trustworthy ground truth: 37-marker Vicon MoCap with human-in-the-loop frame-by-frame cleanup, temporal consistency checks, and SMPL-X reconstruction via SOMA. The paper also reports a meaningful 'effective RPC ratio' (87.0% vs. 6.2% for mmBody), evidencing that the radar is human-centric rather than automotive-oriented, which matters for HMR.

Comprehensive and thoughtfully designed benchmark: three evaluation protocols (P1 in-place, P2 sit-in-place, P3 non-in-place) crossed with three splits (S1 random, S2 cross-subject, S3 cross-action) provide a much richer evaluation than typical single-protocol benchmarks. The inclusion of RPC vs. RT comparison, RGB-D baselines, multimodal fusion, scaling-law analysis, and downstream HAR/HMP is well beyond a token evaluation.

Practical engineering value for the community: the LMDB-based data loading pipeline (lossless sparsity-aware RT compression, byte-stream random access) reduces storage from ~20 TB to ~150 GB and training epoch time from >18 hrs to <1 hr, which substantially lowers the barrier to entry for RT-based research.

Efficient and sensible RT-Mesh baseline: a two-stage design (2D BEV localization + 3D RoI-selected transformer) that avoids prohibitive full-volume 3D/4D convolution, achieving 2.74 ms latency and 2.60 GFLOPs while outperforming adapted RT baselines (RETR, RT-Pose) on most metrics. Useful as a starting point for RT-based HMR.

Clear, well-organized writing with an informative overview figure, dataset comparison table, and strong supplementary documentation (directory structure, action set, implementation details, calibration/synchronization workflow). The privacy motivation and application scenarios (elderly care, rehab, VR gaming) are convincingly argued.

Useful empirical findings that are non-obvious: (i) RT generally generalizes better than RPC on cross-subject/cross-action splits; (ii) radar matches or exceeds depth on translation error and can exceed RGB; (iii) RT+RPC fusion is complementary; (iv) MVE has a clear distance dependence with an optimal 2.0–4.0 m range. These give concrete guidance for future work.
weaknesses: Limited subject and scene diversity for a 'benchmark' paper claiming broad generalizability: only 20 subjects captured in what appears to be a single room/setup within a 6×5.5 m² area. Cross-subject (S2) results show substantial degradation, and there is no cross-environment or cross-device evaluation, so the claim that M4Human 'narrows the gap to RGB-D systems' and supports 'real-world deployment' is only partially substantiated.

The methodological contribution (RT-Mesh) is intentionally minimal—a two-stage localization-then-regression pipeline with straightforward feature concatenation for multimodal fusion. While the authors frame this as encouraging future work, the paper's technical novelty beyond the dataset is modest, and some design choices (e.g., fixed 3D RoI size of 24×24×31, T=4 window) are not ablated or justified quantitatively.

Absolute performance remains weak for the headline HMR task: ~90 mm MVE overall and ~120–135 mm on non-in-place and cross-subject settings, with body-shape parameters (β) noted as inaccurate and 'sometimes inconsistent across frames.' This raises the question of whether radar-based HMR is genuinely ready to support the claimed downstream applications (VR fitness, avatar creation, teleoperation), or whether the benchmark primarily documents difficulty.

Baseline adaptations are somewhat ad hoc: RT-Pose and RETR were originally designed for HPE/detection and are repurposed with HMR heads; it is unclear how much of RT-Mesh's advantage reflects architecture design versus fairness of the adaptation. Similarly, the 4× memory/FLOPs gap favoring RT-Mesh is a design choice (sparse RoI vs. full volume), not necessarily a fundamental property.

Several claims would benefit from more rigorous support: the 'largest' and 'first' claims rest on the comparison table, but no statistical significance testing is provided; the HAR degradation when using RT-predicted (vs. GT) skeletons is reported but not deeply analyzed; and the claimed 'scaling law' is demonstrated over only three data fractions.

Missing or thin details on potential confounders: subject clothing/masks are mentioned for de-identification, but their effect on radar signatures (and thus on HMR) is not discussed; multipath from the single room and chair (explicitly noted in P2) is acknowledged but not quantified; inter-subject annotation consistency for marker placement is not addressed.

strengths: Introduces M4Human, a large-scale multimodal mmWave radar dataset with 661K synchronized frames, 20 subjects, 50 actions, RGB-D, raw radar tensors (RT), radar point clouds (RPC), and marker-based MoCap annotations. This fills a clear gap in radar-based human mesh reconstruction (HMR) benchmarks and supports privacy-preserving human sensing research.

Provides comprehensive benchmark protocols (P1/P2/P3 action groups; S1/S2/S3 splits) and standard metrics (MVE, MJE, MRE, TE), enabling systematic evaluation of in-place, sit-in-place, and non-in-place actions as well as unseen-subject and unseen-action generalization.

Proposes RT-Mesh, a sensible first HMR baseline operating directly on raw radar tensors. The two-stage BEV localization plus 3D RoI transformer design is efficient (2.74 ms latency, 2.6 GFLOPs) and shows stronger cross-subject/cross-action performance than RPC-based alternatives in several settings.

Extensive experiments compare RT vs RPC radar representations, RGB-D baselines, and multimodal fusion. The results provide useful evidence that radar is complementary to RGB/depth, especially for translation/root tracking, and that fusing radar with depth or RGB improves HMR.

The supplementary material gives detailed dataset structure, action taxonomy, implementation details, and qualitative visualizations. The dataset scale analysis (25%/50%/100% training data) supports the claim that larger radar HMR data improves generalization.

The dataset targets meaningful application domains such as rehabilitation, elderly care, smart homes, VR gaming, and privacy-sensitive sensing, and includes diverse non-in-place sports/rehabilitation motions beyond prior in-place-only radar datasets.
weaknesses: Critical dataset construction details lack quantitative validation. Calibration is described qualitatively without reporting reprojection or alignment errors, and time synchronization relies on a manual trigger gesture and manually locating the RGB start frame. For a benchmark paper, this is a material concern because temporal misalignment can directly affect HMR labels and evaluation.

Ground-truth meshes are generated by SOMA from marker trajectories, but no quantitative validation of the resulting SMPL-X meshes is provided beyond visual overlays. Since the benchmark's conclusions depend on GT quality, an error analysis or comparison against independent measurements is needed.

The claimed human motion prediction (HMP) benchmark is unsupported in the provided manuscript: the main text says HMP results are in the supplementary, but the supplementary material shown contains no HMP experiments. Other claimed task supports (human tracking, cross-modal supervision) are also not benchmarked.

Some citation and typographical errors reduce confidence: Table 2 cites P4Transformer as [7] (mmBody) instead of [20]; the text says "adapt RETR [60] from MMVR" in a confusing way; captions contain "crpss-action" and "MoCap-de skeletons." These are minor but indicate insufficient proofreading.

The RT-Mesh baseline is simple, and adapted baselines may not be fully optimized. On S1, RPC P4Transformer is competitive with or slightly better than RT-Mesh on some metrics, so the claimed advantage of RT is not uniformly demonstrated. Stronger baseline tuning or analysis would better support the benchmark claims.

Evaluation breadth is limited: only 20 subjects and 50 single-person actions, no multi-person scenarios, and HAR is evaluated only with radar-derived skeletons. Privacy claims are asserted but not empirically analyzed (e.g., whether raw radar data leaks identity/gait information).
